name: Queen’s Gambit Declined
summary: The QGD (2...e6) supports d5 with a rock-solid structure, one of the soundest defences to 1.d4.
intro: The Queen’s Gambit Declined, 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6, reinforces the d5-pawn and enters some of the most classical positions in chess. Long considered the gold standard of solidity, it has anchored the repertoires of numerous world champions.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Queen's Gambit Declined arises after 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6, one of the most respected and dependable answers to the Queen's Gambit. By supporting the d5-pawn with the e6-pawn, Black builds a firm central foothold that is difficult to break down. The trade-off is that the pawn on e6 temporarily locks in the light-squared bishop on c8, and freeing this piece becomes one of Black's central strategic tasks.

The QGD is prized for its soundness and clarity. Black accepts a slightly passive but resilient position, banking on structural solidity and long-term counterplay. Understanding the interplay between the shut-in bishop and the freeing pawn breaks is the key to handling both sides well.

sections.heading: Typical middlegame
paragraphs: White commonly plays for the central advance e2-e4 or, in structures where a direct break is harder to force, for a minority attack on the queenside. The minority attack sees White push b2-b4-b5 to challenge Black's c6-pawn, aiming to create a weak, backward pawn on an open or half-open c-file that White's pieces can besiege. This slow, positional plan is a defining theme of many QGD structures.

Black's counterplay flows from the freeing breaks ...c5 and ...e5, either of which can open lines for the passive light-squared bishop and relieve the cramped position. Achieving ...e5 under good circumstances is especially liberating, as it strikes at White's center and activates Black's forces. Piece exchanges often ease Black's slightly constricted setup, so timely trades are a recurring resource.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Queen's Gambit Declined has been a mainstay of top-level chess for generations and a staple in the repertoires of many world champions. Its reputation rests on reliability: it gives Black a structurally sound game with well-charted plans against nearly everything White tries. Because the resulting positions reward understanding over memorization, the QGD has long been recommended as a model opening for students of positional chess.

Its many branches, from the classical lines to more modern treatments, share a common strategic backbone built around the d5-point and the fight to free Black's game. This coherence is a large part of why the defense has remained fashionable across changing eras.

keyIdeas: 2...e6 firmly supports d5 and yields one of the soundest defenses to the Queen's Gambit.
The e6-pawn temporarily locks in Black's light-squared bishop, which must later be freed.
White often chooses between the central e4 break and a queenside minority attack.
The minority attack (b4-b5) seeks to create and target a weak black c-pawn.
Black's freeing breaks ...c5 and ...e5 open lines and relieve the cramped position.
Solidity and clear long-term plans make the QGD a model positional opening.

white: Prepare the central break e2-e4 to convert space into an initiative.
Launch a queenside minority attack with b2-b4-b5 to weaken Black's c-pawn.
Pressure the resulting backward c-pawn along a half-open c-file.
Maintain the central bind and restrict Black's shut-in light-squared bishop.
Use space to maneuver pieces to their most active squares.
black: Support the d5-point and keep the structure solid and resilient.
Prepare the freeing break ...c5 or ...e5 to open lines for the bishop.
Develop the light-squared bishop actively once the pawn structure allows.
Seek timely piece exchanges to relieve the slightly cramped position.
Meet a minority attack by defending or timely advancing the queenside pawns.
